summary: A 1976 set of comments from the TENEX implementation of the RCTE Telnet option, which reduces network traffic by deferring transmission of characters that will not cause the receiver to echo. It reports lessons learned in building it.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo records what the TENEX team learned while implementing RCTE for Telnet. It focuses on three cases that made the option difficult to implement correctly.

questions: what problems did tenex find with rcte
subtitle: TENEX implementation notes on three difficulties with the RCTE Telnet option.

tldr.problem: The TENEX implementation of the Remote Controlled Transmission and Echoing option encountered difficult cases involving output, interrupts, and cleared input buffers.
tldr.mechanism: The memo explains how TENEX separated input control from output, marked interrupt positions in the buffer, and used a reset command when the input buffer was cleared.
tldr.outcome: This is an implementation experience note, not the RCTE protocol definition. It records problems and one implementation's responses.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 718's status as Unknown and records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The memo is implementation commentary on the RCTE option.

sections.title: Purpose and Traffic Savings
sections.content:
The RFC circulates a page from notes about changes in Tenex version 1.34. It says the RCTE option's TENEX implementation was complete and shares observations with the network community.

RCTE can reduce traffic by holding characters until one wakes the receiving program. It can also reduce echo traffic: the server tells the user's TELNET program how far it should echo a group of characters, timed so the echo follows the response to the previous group.
sections.plainLanguage: RCTE groups typed characters before sending them, and coordinates when the client echoes them. This can reduce messages in both directions.

sections.title: Spontaneous Output and Interrupts
sections.content:
The memo says the protocol's handling of spontaneous output made a correct implementation extremely difficult. TENEX isolated input-transmission and echo control from output characters, then synchronized the two by embedding control information in the output stream.

RCTE had no explicit interrupt-character mechanism. TENEX treated interrupts as wakeup characters but added a marker at the interrupt's position in the input buffer. The marker was not delivered to the user program or counted as input; a buffer check was changed to account for markers.
sections.plainLanguage: TENEX kept control signals separate from ordinary output. For an interrupt, it placed a marker in the input queue so the program could keep track without receiving a fake character.

sections.title: Resetting a Cleared Buffer
sections.content:
Clearing an input buffer that contains wakeup characters and special markers can leave the user and server TELNET processes out of sync. The memo says it is infeasible to scan the buffer and send a separate RCTE command for every marker.

Instead, TENEX sends WILL RCTE to tell the user TELNET to clear its input buffer and reset counters. This uses the reverse direction from the normal DO RCTE exchange, avoiding a need for another option.
sections.plainLanguage: When the input queue is cleared, one reset command clears the other side's matching state too. That avoids sending a separate correction for every discarded marker.
